rows.title: Eyes
rows.text: A teaching text says most millipedes have a cluster of small eyes on each side of the head, and in one of them, Paraspirobolus lucifugus, each eye has about 20 tiny lens units. Other millipedes have no eyes at all, including the flat-backed millipedes (Polydesmida), the order Platydesmida, and the genus Apheloria. Nobody has counted the eyes of most millipede species, so whether you have eyes, and how many, is unknown.
rows.note: R3 is from an abstract, so I gave only its lens-unit count, rounded to about 20. I did not say which listed species lack eyes, because no record covers them by name.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a blunt-tailed snake millipede, you can resolve a pattern of light and dark bands when one pair of bands spans about 55 degrees, which is enough to detect a dark object 20 degrees across. A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, a pattern thousands of times finer. Nobody has measured how sharply other millipedes see, though a close relative in the same genus, Cylindroiulus, very likely sees as coarsely.
rows.note: Only Cylindroiulus punctatus is measured (R1, from a 56° period); the other species' sharpness is stated as unmeasured.

rows.title: Light through the skin
rows.text: Your skin may sense light all over your body. If you are a greenhouse millipede, an experiment found that your skin senses light and that light changes how much you move, without steering you toward or away from it. Nobody has measured whether other millipedes sense light through the skin.
rows.note: Removed the year. R1's quote says "both species" without naming the second, so I named only the greenhouse millipede. R1 does not say whether light speeds you up or slows you down, so I left that out.

rows.title: Touch
rows.text: In the order Polydesmida, a walking millipede keeps touching the ground with the tips of its antennae. If you are a Paradesmus gracilis, you have tactile hairs on your legs, on the sides of your body and especially on your antennae, and reactions to touch count for a great deal in what you do. Nobody has measured how light a touch you can feel.
rows.note: Replaced the flagged word. R1 quote is cut off, so I used only the hair locations and the importance of contact reactions. R2's count of antennal tip structures is cut off, so I left it out.

rows.title: Taste and damp
rows.text: If you are a Paradesmus gracilis, odors get no response from you, but glucose and sucrose attract you when you touch them. Moisture matters far more in your behavior than humidity does, and your response to it is a change in how fast you move, probably a general effect of dehydration. Nobody has measured how other millipedes sense taste or damp.
rows.note: Removed the year. Left out R3 (Tömösváry organs, an order-level thought) and the sugar threshold number, which has no job.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have, or which colors they pick up. Nobody can yet say whether you see color at all.
rows.note: No records were supplied, so the row only states that nothing has been measured; I left out any claim about millipede eyes or light sensing.

failed.title: Night
errors: the number 2022 is in none of the cited records
failed.last: One millipede, Paraspirobolus lucifugus, moves away from light and is active only at night, and its daily rhythm is apparently run by an internal clock, according to the abstract of a 2022 paper by Meyer-Rochow. Nobody has recorded whether you are active at night or by day.
